questions.question: A page displays a name taken from the URL query string. Which line is safe from XSS?
questions.explanation: textContent always treats the value as plain text, while innerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML and document.write parse it as HTML and can run injected handlers.

questions.question: After `merge({}, JSON.parse('{"__proto__": {"isAdmin": true}}'))` with a naive recursive merge, what does `({}).isAdmin` return?
options: true, because the merge wrote isAdmin onto Object.prototype
questions.explanation: JSON.parse keeps __proto__ as an own key, but target['__proto__'] in the merge reaches the real prototype, so every object inherits isAdmin: true.

questions.question: Which is the strongest defence for storing user-controlled keys without prototype pollution risk?
options: Using Object.assign instead of a loop
Using a Map or an object created with Object.create(null)
questions.explanation: A Map does not treat keys as properties, and Object.create(null) has no prototype to reach, so special keys like __proto__ are just data.

questions.question: What does `npm ci` do that makes it preferable to `npm install` in CI pipelines?
options: It upgrades every dependency to the newest version
It installs exactly the versions pinned in package-lock.json and fails if the lockfile is out of sync
It removes all install scripts from packages permanently
It scans the code for XSS vulnerabilities
questions.explanation: npm ci gives reproducible installs from the committed lockfile, so an unexpected new (possibly malicious) version cannot slip in silently.
